Our smallest models run on budget phones, wearables, and Raspberry Pis. No GPU, no server, and no data leaving the device.
Needle 3 demo: none of the user's queries worked, including "more light", "less light", "both doors should be locked", and "if blinds are open, open back door".

Indirect home commands failed. "I need a wee" played music (treating 'wee' as a genre), "I need a wee wee" started the vacuum in the bathroom, and a 'too dark' request set the living room lights to an invalid 'dark' value instead of lighting the bathroom.

"Turn all the lights on/off" and "it's too dark in the bathroom" worked, but less direct phrasing didn't. "It's too cold" and "make it hot" turned the thermostat down, the latter with high confidence. In the laptop demo, "check mail" and "open email" misfired while "open mail" worked. The reasoning output isn't trustworthy.
From limited testing, Needle 3 can handle up to about 10 tools/definitions; beyond that it gets confused.
Confidence scores aren't reliable. "Turn the kitchen to 230°C" executed with 0.90 confidence, and "My car crashed I need help" on the phone model triggered play_music with confidence 1.
Tried Needle 3 for labelling and it was very bad; MNLI did better. One user concluded you need to match the use case exactly.
Needle 3 doesn't run inference on Apple GPU; GPU is used only for training.
"Illuminate/de-illuminate (roomname)" works well, and "harden perimeter" locks the doors and sets the alarm.
"Warm the house" set the lights to a warm brightness instead of raising the thermostat. The user would rather have exact phrase-to-control mappings than a heuristic model.

A user's RuneScape database tool-calling benchmark showed Needle 3 is a solid improvement over Needle 2 but still far behind FunctionGemma. Fine-tuned Needle 3 W4A8 got 32.2% correct tool shape and 20.4% exact arguments, versus FunctionGemma's 90.9%/85.2% and Needle 2's 25.7%/18.7%.

Asking it to both turn up the home temperature and turn down the living room lights produced a clean JSON doc. Paired with a small Whisper/Parakeet voice model, the user sees use cases in low-power settings like car, marine, home, and industrial.
Performance is quite good even on CPU, but on a Pixel the GPU isn't used even when enabled. The user had previously been running models in Termux.

Android chat app compared to another app tried a year ago: fast and accurate on math, translation, and movie trivia, and called the fastest offline LLM seen on that phone. Issues: it sometimes repeats the last phrase endlessly, and the chat doesn't auto-scroll to follow the answer.
Critic: Cactus vendored llama.cpp yet still calls itself "Ollama for *".
Ollama already runs fine on Android via Termux with 5GB models and now has a package, so there's no need to compile from source.
The API is very simple. The user had tried on-device LLMs in Swift with LLM.swift, which went okay, and was excited to try Cactus in React Native.
Demo app feedback: no dark mode and low-contrast text are accessibility problems. Downloading Jan Nano or SmolLM3 via the GGUF link worked, but the app crashed immediately on selecting them.

API critique: models download inline at runtime. Mobile apps usually block on a first-run progress bar, so developers want a separate download-or-cache API that returns an identifier to pass into inference.
A user integrated Cactus Hybrid (Gemma 4 with a confidence score) into a mic transcription project for fun, running it on a Framework Desktop.
Critique of the "knows when it's wrong" framing: a model can only detect uncertainty or inconsistency, not wrongness. The commenter suggests describing the confidence score differently.
